newsitem.title: TURKEY: Politics triggers volatility in Turkish markets.
newsitem.headline: Politics triggers volatility in Turkish markets.

text.p: Mounting political concerns in Turkey, ignited by uncertainities over the future of the Islamist-led government, have increased volatility in Turkish markets.
Denial by Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller of a press story that she would pull out of the alliance helped Istanbul stocks recover part of its two-day losses in afternoon trading.
But brokers say the market is still cautious ahead of a key meeting of the military-dominated National Security Council (NSC) on Saturday.
The IMKB National-100, which dived 4.9 percent on Thursday over fears the coalition government may collapse, closed at 1,466, up 0.62 percent.
"I'm not very hopeful. Stock prices may fall or remain sidelined for a while. An uptrend is unlikely," said Ertan Gungor, assistant general manager of Tekstil Bank.

"Prices may fall further if the government collapses," he added. But some brokers believe the collapse of Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Islamist-led coalition and the possibility of the establishment of a new one would end uncertainities and boost stock prices.
Bond rates rose about two percentage points to 99 percent after a four percent increase on Thursday.
Some bankers say any possibility of early elections might trigger further rate hikes in financial markets which have remained stable so far despite rate fluctuations.

"Bonds rates have reached their peak, reflecting the recent political developments. For a further rise, there must be a possibility of early elections this year," said the treasurer of an Istanbul-based private bank.
Ali Ozenc, treasurer of private Finansbank, said an early election or a military intervention would be the most negative outcome of the ongoing political crisis for financial markets.
"The collapse of the government or the establishment of a new one do not distort financial stability...The worst of all would be an early election or a military rule," Ozenc said.

Turkey's chief of staff Ismail Hakki Karadayi said on Friday the army -- which has ousted three civilian governments since 1960 -- was watching political developments closely and demanded parliament act to resolve the political deadlock gripping Ankara.
But he pledged to keep the soldiers out of politics, state-run Anatolian news agency reported.
Mehmet Yildirim, head of Istanbul's Chamber of Commerce, blamed the political turmoil for hampering the economy and urged parliament to end the crisis soon.
The lira closed at 134,000 against the dollar thanks to the central bank's interventionsin in the past two days which bankers said had weakened the demand for the U.S. currency.
"Erbakan's delaying tactics keeps the market waiting. But in the end, it must be accepted that the coalition government is in a tight corner," said Tuncay Kuzu from Sahin securities.
Brokers said the underlying mood would continue to be jittery unless the political upheavel settles and the NSC meeting produces a reconciliation.
"The market is waiting for the result of the NSC meeting in the short-term. The market trend may be clear on Monday," said Korhan Biricik from Deha Securities.
The military members of the NSC are expected to increase demands on the reluctant government to implement anti-Islamist measures introduced by the generals at a February meeting.
The government has taken no concrete steps to comply with the army's demands, which include restrictions on religious education, and strict enforcement of bans on Islamic dress.
